# Introduction
Diabetes mellitus (commonly referred to as just diabetes) is a metabolic disorder in which there is a lack of insulin secretation or development of insulin resistance (or a combination of both). The lack of insulin or response to insulin prevents the body from regulating blood glucose levels properly leading to development of a condition known as hyperglycemia. Short-term symptoms of hyperglycemia including dehydration, fatigue or weakness, and blurred vision. Hyperglycemia is also dangerous, as long-term effects include kidney damage, heart disease, and poor wound healing leading to a much higher risk of infections. Diabetes can classified as type 1 or type 2, with type 1 resulting from a lack of or no insulin production. Type 2 diabetes results from the body developing a resistance to insulin leading to the pancreas not being able to produce enough insulin. Depending on the type of diabetes a patient may require prescribed insulin and consistent blood glucose monitoring. [Source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332223015329?via%3Dihub)

Diabetes has a large impact on the health of Canadians, in 2023 to 2024 the Public Health Agency of Canada found that [3.9 million Canadians](https://health-infobase.canada.ca/diabetes/) live with diagnosed diabetes. Diabetes is ranked 7th in leading causes of death in Canada, with more than [6,874 deaths](https://doi.org/10.25318/1310039401-eng) diabetes related deaths in 2024 alone. Aside from health impacts, diabetes also has a significant financial burden on Canadians, in 2024 the costs of diabetes on the Canadian healthcare system totalled to [$18.25 billion](https://www.diabetes.ca/what-is-diabetes/diabetes-in-canada). 

From a public health perspective it is important to understand the impact of diabetes on Canadian as it can allow for more equitable allocation of health resources and better preventative education. Comparing provinces, [Statistics Canada](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/82-570-x/2024001/section2-eng.htm) report diabetes as more common in Newfoundland and Labrador (11.1%) and Nova Scotia (10.5%) when compared to British Columbia (6.8%). In the same report, diabetes is also much more prevalent in Canadians with a disability (16.6%) than those without (6.9%). [Overweight and obesity are both risk factors for diabetes](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/82-570-x/2024001/section2-eng.htm), with body mass index (BMI) being one method of classifying body weight in relation to health risk. Understanding the impact of risk factors on diabetes prevalence can educate the public on developing healthy habits in order to minimize the development of diabetes. Understanding these regional variations in diabetes prevalence and its effect on Canadians is important to providing equitable healthcare and informing public health decisions. 

Our analysis aims to investigate the ability of using BMI as a predictor of diabetes status in Canadians. [Previous literature](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/pub/82-003-x/2008003/article/10680-eng.pdf?st=K5h3zTVe) has found that when BMI values were correctly reported they provide a good measure of obesity prevalence. The ability of using BMI as a predictor of diabetes status supports obesisty being a key risk factor and BMI representing this risk. Our model provides insight into the risks associated with diabetes, while also providing better understanding on the strength of those risks. A model mapping the association between BMI and diabetes status can help inform health decisions and policy regarding diabetes.

# Methods

## Applying BMI to predict diabetes status


```{python}
# select the target and prediction feature
df = df[["BMI", "Diabetes_binary"]]

# split data in train and test, stratify is to ensure there are enough examples in both splits
# because most examples are non diabetic
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(
    df,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=522,
    stratify=df["Diabetes_binary"]
)
# Create processed data directory
processed_dir = Path("../data/processed")
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# save the files and check the df shapes
train_df.to_csv(processed_dir / "train.csv", index=False)
test_df.to_csv(processed_dir / "test.csv", index=False)

print("Training shape:", train_df.shape)
print("Testing shape:", test_df.shape)
```

```{python}
# BMI summary by diabetes status using training data
bmi_summary = train_df.groupby("Diabetes_binary")["BMI"].agg(
    ["count", "mean", "median", "std"]
)
```

## Body mass index (BMI) as a predictor of diabetes

Rafiq, Shamaila, and Per Bendix Jeppesen. 2018. "Body Mass Index, Vitamin D, and Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." Nutrients 10 (9): 1182. <https://doi.org/10.3390/nu10091182>.

High body mass index (BMI) is strongly associated with diabetes (https://doi.org/10.3390/nu10091182). Based on this, we first compared the distribution of BMI between individuals who have been diagnosed with diabetes and those who have not (Figure 1).

```{python}
# sample training data for the plot
plot_df = train_df.sample(n=10000, random_state=522).copy()

# The following plot was made using GPT6 for assistance.
plot_df["Diabetes status"] = plot_df["Diabetes_binary"].map({
    0: "No diabetes",
    1: "Diabetes"
})

# Compare BMI distributions
bmi_plot = alt.Chart(plot_df, width=600, height=300).transform_density(
    "BMI",
    groupby=["Diabetes status"]
).mark_area(opacity=0.6).encode(
    x=alt.X("value:Q", title="Body Mass Index (BMI)"),
    y=alt.Y("density:Q", stack=False, title="Density"),
    color=alt.Color("Diabetes status:N")
).properties(
    title="BMI Distribution by Diabetes Status"
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bmi-distribution
#| fig-cap: "BMI distribution by diabetes status from train data."
bmi_plot
```

Figure 1 shows that the BMI distribution for individuals with diabetes is shifted toward higher values compared with those without diabetes. This supports our choice of BMI as a predictor of diabetes status.

```{python}
# BMI summary by diabetes status using training data
bmi_summary
```

```{python}
# select BMI as the prediction feature and diabetes as the target
X_train = train_df[["BMI"]]
y_train = train_df["Diabetes_binary"]

X_test = test_df[["BMI"]]
y_test = test_df["Diabetes_binary"]

# create the logistic regression model
logistic_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)
```

```{python}
# compare regular and balanced logistic regression
param_grid_logistic = {
    "logisticregression__class_weight": [None, "balanced"]
}

# use F1 score to balance precision and recall
logistic_search = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=logistic_model,
    param_grid=param_grid_logistic,
    cv=3,
    scoring="f1",
    n_jobs=-1
)

# train the model
logistic_search.fit(X_train, y_train)

# check the best parameters and F1 score
print("Best parameters:", logistic_search.best_params_)
print("Best CV F1:", logistic_search.best_score_)
```

```{python}
# predict diabetes using the test data
logistic_pred = logistic_search.predict(X_test)
```


```{python}
# calculate accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score
logistic_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, logistic_pred)
logistic_precision = precision_score(y_test, logistic_pred, zero_division=0)
logistic_recall = recall_score(y_test, logistic_pred, zero_division=0)
logistic_f1 = f1_score(y_test, logistic_pred, zero_division=0)

# save results
score_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Accuracy": [logistic_accuracy],
    "Precision": [logistic_precision],
    "Recall": [logistic_recall],
    "F1 Score": [logistic_f1]
}, index=["Test set"])
```

```{python}
# compare the predicted and actual diabetes status
confusion_matrix = pd.crosstab(
    y_test,
    logistic_pred,
    rownames=["Actual diabetes status"],
    colnames=["Predicted diabetes status"]
)
```

```{python}
# accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score in a df
score_results
```

```{python}
# confusion matrix in a df
confusion_matrix
```

The logistic regression model has an accuracy of 67.62% and an F1 score of 0.3360. on the test data. The model correctly idetified 4156 diabetes positive cases but also failed to identify 2913 cases resulting in a recall of 58.79%.

The model also produced 13514 false positives, suggesting that BMI alone is not sufficient for reliable diabetes classification. Although the model identifies more than half of the diabetes true positives, its low precision and high false negative make it unsuitable as is for medical screening.

## The limitation of our model because our model is underperforming compared to Gold Standard

## Our model should not be used to diagnose diabetes

## Our model does not account for other features associated with diabetes

Ismail, Leila, Huned Materwala, and Juma Al Kaabi. 2021. “Association of Risk Factors with Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review.” Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal 19: 1759–1785. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csbj.2021.03.003.

Our model uses body mass index (BMI) as its only feature to predict diabetes status. As a result, it leaves out many other factors associated with diabetes, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, sleep, family history, and ethnicity [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csbj.2021.03.003]. Without these factors, our model greatly oversimplifies the range of factors associated with diabetes.

## Potentially improving our predictive model

Adding other features associated with diabetes [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csbj.2021.03.003], such as, but not limited to, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and smoking status, could improve our model's ability to predict diabetes.

We explored only two model types, k-nearest neighbours (kNN) and logistic regression, to predict diabetes status from a single feature, BMI. Trying other models, and tuning their hyperparameters, could make our predictions more accurate and robust.
